title: Deduction: must, might, may, could, can't
tagline: From 'no way' to 'definitely' — five modal verbs for guessing what's true.
why: Deduction modals turn up constantly in the open cloze and in the collaborative Speaking task, where you have to reason out loud about a picture or a situation together with your partner. Getting must, might, could and can't in the right order of certainty — and adding have + past participle for a guess about the past — is exactly the kind of natural, spoken grammar the exam rewards.

hook.text: Liam: “Did you hear that? It might be an animal outside!” Nadia: “Relax, it can't be anything dangerous — we're inside the fence.” Sofia: “It must be the wind in the trees.”
hook.ask: Three friends guess what's making the noise, but with different levels of certainty. Which guess sounds most sure, which sounds least sure, and which is a confident 'no way'?

items.label: might be / may be / could be

diagrams.title: Build the sentence

sentences.note: past deduction — must have + past participle

diagrams.caption: The modal goes straight before be, or before have + past participle for a guess about the past — never with to.

use.point: must for present deduction — almost certain

examples.text: It's midnight and the light is on — Miss Vega must be still awake.
examples.note: strong evidence, an almost certain conclusion

examples.text: You've walked for six hours — you must be exhausted.
That noise must be an owl — we heard one earlier.
It's dark, so it might be a fox out there.
The noise could be a branch falling — hard to tell.
examples.note: could = also possible, similar to might

examples.text: It can't be dangerous — we're safely inside the fence.
examples.note: the opposite of must — impossible, not just unlikely

examples.text: Nadia can't be asleep already; it's only nine o'clock.

use.point: deduction about the past: must have / might have / can't have + participle

examples.text: Someone must have eaten all the snacks — the bag is empty!
examples.note: an almost certain conclusion about something in the past

examples.text: Liam might have dropped his torch near the tent.
examples.note: a possible explanation for a past event

examples.text: It can't have been a bear — there aren't any bears here.

watch_out.wrong: It must to be the wind.
watch_out.why: Modals for deduction go straight before be/have — no to.

watch_out.wrong: It can be a bear, we're safe here.
watch_out.right: It can't be a bear — we're safe here.
watch_out.why: Can on its own doesn't mean impossible; the negative can't is the deduction form for 'impossible'.
Deduction about the past needs must have + past participle, not the simple past.

watch_out.wrong: You must be tired, go and clean your tent now.
watch_out.right: You must be tired — rest for a while.
watch_out.why: Deduction must (a guess) is different from obligation must (an order) — don't confuse the two.

watch_out.wrong: It might have to be an animal.
watch_out.why: No to after a deduction modal — might/may/could go straight before be.

watch_out.wrong: It can't have be a bear.
watch_out.why: Past deduction needs have + been (the participle of be), not have + be.

l1.why: Spanish debe de + infinitivo becomes must + base verb in English, with no to and no de.
Spanish no puede ser (impossible) is can't be in English, not the positive can.

l1.es: Debió de habérselos comido él mismo.
l1.why: Deduction about a past event needs must have + participle, not the simple past.

l1.es: Puede que se le cayera la linterna.
l1.wrong: He can have dropped his torch.
l1.why: Puede que for a guess about the past is might/could have + participle, not can have.

remember.trick: can't → might → must: impossible to certain!
remember.tip: Say the sentence with sure, maybe or no way instead of the modal — if it still makes sense, you've picked the right one.

dialogue.title: The noise outside the tent
dialogue.context: On a school camping trip in the mountains, Mateo, Sofia, Liam and Nadia hear a strange noise at night.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Did you hear that? It might be an animal outside!

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Relax, it can't be anything dangerous — we're inside the fence.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: It must be the wind in the trees.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Or it could be Miss Vega checking the tents.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Wait — my snack bag is empty! Someone must have eaten everything!

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: It can't have been me, I was asleep by nine.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: It might have been a fox — they love food like that.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Or you must have eaten it yourself and forgotten, Liam!

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: No way! I can't have eaten a whole bag that fast.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Whatever it was, it must be gone by now — let's sleep.

It ___ dangerous — we're safely inside the fence.
Someone ___ all the snacks — the bag is empty!

It ___ a bear — there aren't any bears here.

items.first: I'm almost certain that noise is the wind.
Maybe it's a fox outside — we can't be sure.
It's impossible for it to be dangerous — we're safe.
I'm sure someone ate all the snacks.
It's impossible that it was a bear — there aren't any here.

can_do: I can guess about the present with must, might/may/could and can't.
I can guess about the past with must have, might have and can't have + past participle.
I can tell the difference between deduction must (a guess) and obligation must (a rule).
summary: Must be / must have been = an almost certain guess, based on strong evidence.
Might/may/could be = a real possibility, not certain.
Can't be / can't have been = a confident 'impossible', the opposite of must.
For the past, add have + past participle: must have left, might have dropped, can't have been.
Deduction must (a guess) is different from obligation must (a rule) — check the context.
